newsitem.title: USA: Key senator sees need for budget amendment change.
newsitem.headline: Key senator sees need for budget amendment change.

text.p: The fate in the Senate of the balanced budget amendment to the U.S. Constitution has come down to a lone Democrat, Sen. Robert Torricelli of New Jersey, who said Wednesday the amendment needed major changes.

Torricelli, who has scheduled a news conference later in the day to announce his position on the amendment, did not say whether he would vote for or against the Republican version if his proposed changes were not accepted.
"I believe the ... amendment would be improved and enhanced by these changes. Indeed, I believe these changes are necessary," Torricelli said in a speech on the Senate floor.

Republican sponsors believe they have 66 committed votes but need one more to pass the historic amendment with a two-third majority in the Senate. Torricelli was the last senator whose position was unknown.

House Republican leaders hoped passage in the Senate would boost its chances among their own members. The amendment bogged down when several Republicans said they could not go along with their leaders unless the Social Security retirement program's funds were protected from cuts.
Senate Republicans said the Social Security issue was political cover raised by the White House and Democrats for those who do not want to vote for the amendment.

Republicans were counting on Torricelli, who won in November after one of the year's most negative Senate campaigns, to stand by his campaign pledge to vote for a balanced budget amendment. He voted for a similar measure in the House in 1995.

It failed in the Senate that year by one vote but supporters believed chances were good this year because of the election to the Senate of Torricelli and others who backed the constitutional amendment in the House.
Torricelli's proposed changes would create a separate capital budget for infrastructure spending and make it easier for Congress to vote for deficit spending in time of recession or war.
"Amending the Constitution is unlike any other action taken by the Congress," he said. "These are words that will govern contingencies that we cannot imagine, circumstances that we cannot foresee."

The amendment would require Washington to balance its books annually starting in 2002 or within two years of its enactment, but it does not specify how Congress is to balance the budget and would permit deficits and borrowing if approved by three-fifths of Congress.
Within seven years of clearing Congress the amendment must be ratified by 38 of 50 states to become part of the Constitution.
